common_name: Buzz Ivory Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Cream-White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Ivory stays compact enough for patio pots and small borders without the sprawl of full-size davidii selections.

directions: Part of the Buzz series bred to condense full-size butterfly bush flower spikes onto a noticeably shorter, denser framework, Buzz Ivory carries slender panicles of creamy white blooms from midsummer into fall on a fountain-shaped shrub roughly a third smaller than older davidii cultivars. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since rich soil or excess shade encourages loose, floppy growth at the expense of flower density. Cut the framework back hard to a few inches above the ground in late winter each year to keep the plant compact and to trigger the strongest flush of new flowering wood. Its smaller footprint suits mixed containers and tight border spots where a full-size butterfly bush would need constant restraint.

common_name: Buzz Velvet Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Deep Purple-Red Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Velvet's compact scale fits smaller beds and large containers better than standard butterfly bush.

directions: Buzz Velvet is the darkest-flowered member of the Buzz series, opening deep wine-purple, almost burgundy blooms in dense conical spikes against gray-green foliage on a shrub kept notably shorter than older Buddleja davidii selections. Grow in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, where lean conditions keep the habit tight and heavily flowered rather than lax. Prune the entire framework back hard in late winter, since flowers form only on new season's growth and this cutback is what keeps the compact scale that distinguishes the Buzz series from full-size butterfly bush. Deadheading spent spikes through summer extends the bloom season and keeps the deep color coming steadily until frost.

common_name: Lo & Behold Purple Haze Butterfly Bush (Wide-Spreading Sterile Lavender-Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Purple Haze spreads considerably wider than it grows tall, so allow extra lateral room compared with upright Buddleja cultivars.

directions: Unlike the mounding, roughly equal-dimension habit of most dwarf Buddleja, Purple Haze from the Lo & Behold series spreads low and wide, forming a groundcover-like mat that can reach a foot or more across for every foot of height, and is useful for covering slopes or filling wide bed fronts where an upright shrub would leave gaps. Fragrant bluish-lavender flower spikes cover the spreading branches from summer into fall and, like other Lo & Behold selections, the plant is bred to be sterile, producing little to no viable seed. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun and cut the entire plant back hard in late winter to keep it dense and to renew flowering wood, since old stems bloom less vigorously. Its low, wide form also makes it a strong candidate for mixed containers where trailing growth over the pot edge is wanted.

common_name: Free Petite Blue Heaven Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Reblooming Lavender-Blue Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Free Petite Blue Heaven is bred for a rounded, very compact habit that suits small beds and patio containers.

directions: Free Petite Blue Heaven packs full-size, fragrant lavender-blue flower spikes onto one of the smallest butterfly bush frameworks bred to date, forming a tidy rounded mound well under three feet at maturity. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since overly rich soil produces soft growth and fewer flowers. It reblooms continuously from early summer through frost with only light deadheading of spent spikes, and its diminutive scale makes it one of the few butterfly bush selections well suited to small urban gardens, foundation plantings, and large patio containers. Cut the whole plant back hard in late winter to renew flowering wood and maintain its compact form.

common_name: Purple Cloud Agapanthus (Dense Dark Violet-Purple Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Purple Cloud produces exceptionally dense flower heads on sturdy upright stalks that hold well without staking.

directions: Purple Cloud is grown for having among the darkest, most saturated flower color of any widely available agapanthus, with tightly packed umbels of deep violet-purple pendulous trumpets held well above the strap-shaped foliage on stiff, upright stalks in mid to late summer. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, watering regularly through the growing season but tapering off once flowering finishes to help the deciduous foliage die back cleanly for winter. Established clumps flower most heavily when left undisturbed and only moderately crowded, so avoid dividing more often than every three to four years. In colder parts of its range, mulch the dormant crown over winter to protect it from hard freezes.

common_name: Navy Blue Agapanthus (Deep Royal-Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Navy Blue is one of the most widely planted deep-blue agapanthus selections in European gardens and performs reliably in typical border conditions.

directions: Navy Blue produces medium-sized umbels of rich, dark royal-blue trumpet flowers on sturdy stalks that stand well above the clump of strap-shaped deciduous foliage, opening in midsummer and continuing for several weeks. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and water deeply through the growing season while allowing the soil to dry between waterings, since soggy winter conditions are more damaging than drought. Its reliable, long-blooming display and dependable habit have made it a standard border and mass-planting selection, and clumps reward being left to fill in for several seasons before division. Where winters are borderline for its hardiness range, a dry mulch layer over the dormant crown improves survival.

common_name: Midnight Cascade Agapanthus (Tall Near-Black-Budded Drooping Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Midnight Cascade sends up tall flowering stalks well above the foliage, so site it toward the back of a border or stake in windy locations.

directions: A deciduous selection of the drooping species Agapanthus inapertus, Midnight Cascade opens from near-black buds into rich dark purple, narrow trumpet flowers that hang downward from the umbel rather than facing outward like most garden agapanthus, giving flowering stalks that can reach five feet an unusually somber, elegant character. Grow in full sun in humus-rich, well-drained soil, and let the foliage die back fully each autumn, since this deciduous habit is part of what gives inapertus selections greater cold tolerance than evergreen agapanthus. The tall, relatively slender flower stalks benefit from a sheltered spot or discreet staking in exposed gardens. Established clumps flower best when left undivided for several years and given a dry winter mulch at the colder end of their range.

common_name: Golden Drop Agapanthus (Gold-Margined Variegated Foliage Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Golden Drop holds its gold leaf margins best with some protection from the harshest midday sun in hot climates.

directions: Golden Drop is grown chiefly for its grey-green strap leaves edged in a bright, buttery-yellow margin, a variegation pattern that gives the compact evergreen clump season-long ornamental value well before the pale blue summer umbels open on sturdy upright stalks. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; some afternoon shade in hot inland climates keeps the gold edging from bleaching out. Groom out any leaves that revert to plain green promptly at the base to keep the clump true to its variegated form, and avoid dividing until clumps are well filled in, since both foliage color and flowering improve with a little congestion. Its smaller, tidy scale suits containers and foliage-driven mixed plantings as much as its flowers suit a summer border.
